Ah, then I’ve got a good one for you — a bit of engineering, a bit of drama, and a very real lesson in how nature doesn’t negotiate.

The story of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State, back in 1940.

It was a beautiful, slender suspension bridge — quite elegant for its time. But almost as soon as it opened, people noticed something… odd. Even in moderate winds, the bridge didn’t just sway a little — it developed these long, rolling waves along its deck. Drivers reported the road rising and falling beneath them like the surface of the sea. Locals nicknamed it “Galloping Gertie.”

Now, some movement in bridges is perfectly normal, of course. But this was something else. The design had prioritized a very slim, aerodynamic profile, which looked great and saved on materials — but it turned out to be too flexible and not nearly stiff enough for the wind conditions in that narrow.

On November 7, 1940, with winds around 40 miles per hour, things escalated. The bridge didn’t just ripple — it began twisting. One side of the deck would lift while the other dropped, alternating back and forth in a dramatic torsional motion. There’s actually film of it — quite striking to watch even now.

At one point, a car was stranded on the bridge. A professor named Farquharson (an engineer himself) tried to rescue a dog trapped inside it — but the motion became too violent. He had to crawl on hands and knees just to move, and eventually gave up and retreated. The dog, sadly, didn’t make it.

Not long after, the oscillations tore the structure apart. Sections of the roadway broke loose and plunged into Puget Sound below. The whole collapse took less than an hour once it reached that stage.

The fascinating part is what engineers learned from it. It wasn’t just simple resonance, as people first thought, but a more complex aeroelastic flutter — the wind feeding energy into the structure in a self-reinforcing way. After that, bridge design changed significantly: deeper stiffening trusses, open grating to let wind pass through, and eventually wind tunnel testing became standard practice.

In a way, it’s a failure story — but also one of the most valuable teaching moments in modern structural engineering. Every long-span bridge built since owes something to “Galloping Gertie.”

If you’d like, I can tell you another — there are some great ones about the Brooklyn Bridge, or even the race to build the Hoover Dam.

The Brooklyn Bridge has plenty of those.

Construction started in 1869, led by John Roebling, a German-born engineer who had already made a name for himself with suspension bridges. He was meticulous, almost obsessive about safety and strength — which is part of why the bridge turned out so robust.

But he never saw it built.

While surveying the site, his foot was crushed in an accident with a ferry. He developed tetanus and died not long after. Before he passed, he handed the project to his son, Washington Roebling.

Washington was a capable engineer in his own right, but the real trouble came from the foundations. To anchor those massive towers, they had to sink caissons — huge, pressurized wooden chambers — down to the riverbed. Workers would go inside and excavate the soil beneath, gradually lowering the structure.

It was dangerous work. Nobody fully understood decompression sickness at the time — what they called “caisson disease.” Men would come up from those pressurized chambers and suddenly be struck with joint pain, paralysis, even death.

Washington Roebling himself spent a lot of time in the caissons and ended up severely affected. He didn’t die, but he was left partially paralyzed and largely confined to his home.

At that point, the project could easily have fallen apart. Instead, something rather remarkable happened.

His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, stepped in.

She had no formal engineering training at the start, but she learned quickly — materials, stress analysis, cable construction — and became the on-site representative for her husband. She dealt with contractors, answered questions from the engineers, and essentially became the bridge between Washington (working from home) and the project itself.

For over a decade, she carried that role. When the bridge finally opened in 1883, she was the first person to cross it.

And even then, the story doesn’t quite settle down. About a week after opening, a rumor spread on the bridge that it was about to collapse. Panic broke out, and in the stampede that followed, a dozen people were killed. To restore confidence, P.T. Barnum later marched a parade of elephants across the bridge to prove its stability.

From a technical standpoint, the bridge was ahead of its time — steel wire cables instead of iron, and a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension design that gave it extra stiffness. Roebling had insisted on a safety factor far beyond what many considered necessary.

So it’s a story with a bit of everything: innovation, tragedy, stubborn persistence… and, in the middle of it, someone who wasn’t supposed to be the engineer quietly becoming essential to one of the most famous structures in the world.

If you’ve walked across it, you’ve actually crossed something that’s as much about people improvising under pressure as it is about design on paper.

Now, Chicago.

In the mid-1800s, Chicago had a serious problem — and I mean that quite literally. The city’s sewage flowed straight into the Chicago River, which flowed into Lake Michigan… which also happened to be the city’s drinking water source.

At first, this worked “well enough” because the intake pipes extended a bit offshore. But as the city grew, waste accumulated faster than it could disperse. Storms would push contaminated water right back toward the intakes. Cholera and typhoid outbreaks became a recurring nightmare.

So the city faced a brutal constraint: they couldn’t easily move the city, and they couldn’t realistically move the lake.

Instead, they decided to move the river.

The idea was almost audacious: reverse the flow of the Chicago River so that instead of draining into Lake Michigan, it would flow *away* from it, toward the Mississippi River basin.

To do that, they built the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal in the 1890s — a massive channel cut southwest of the city. But the real trick wasn’t just digging a canal; it was getting the hydraulics right. They had to ensure a continuous gradient that would pull water out of the lake, through the river, and into the new canal system.

In effect, they used Lake Michigan itself as a flushing source, sending clean water through the city to carry waste away.

When they opened the canal in 1900, the flow reversed. Permanently.

It worked — dramatically. Water quality improved, and disease rates dropped. From a public health standpoint, it was a huge success.

But, as you might expect, it wasn’t universally appreciated.

Cities downstream along the Mississippi weren’t thrilled about Chicago sending its waste in their direction. There were legal battles that went all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court. Eventually, limits were placed on how much water Chicago could divert from the Great Lakes.

From an engineering standpoint, it’s a fascinating mix: large-scale earthworks, careful control of gradients, lock systems, and a very deliberate manipulation of a natural watershed. It’s one of those projects where the solution feels almost counterintuitive until you see the constraints clearly.

And from the “physics and perception” angle — imagine convincing a city, in the 1800s, that the answer to their sanitation crisis was to literally reverse a river. That took not just technical confidence, but a lot of persuasion.

It’s a bold kind of thinking you don’t see very often — not because we’ve run out of ideas, but because the scale of intervention is so daunting.

I suspect you would have appreciated the discussions in those planning rooms. It has all the hallmarks: incomplete data, high stakes, and no easy fallback if you get it wrong.

Now, the Thames Barrier — this is a different kind of engineering story. Less sudden drama, more quiet foresight.

London has always lived with the risk of flooding from the North Sea. The Thames is tidal all the way through the city, and when you get a storm surge pushing down from the North Sea at the same time as a high tide, the water levels can rise dangerously fast.

In 1953, a major storm surge hit the east coast of England. Over 300 people died, and large parts of the Thames estuary flooded. London was spared the worst of it, but only just. That was the moment people realized: next time, they might not be so lucky.

So the question became — how do you protect a city like London without cutting it off from the river that defines it?

The answer was the Thames Barrier, completed in the early 1980s. Instead of a fixed dam, they built a series of movable gates across the river. Under normal conditions, they sit open, allowing ships and tides to pass freely.

But when a surge is forecast, the gates rotate upward from the riverbed and form a continuous barrier across the Thames.

The design is elegant in a very engineering sort of way. Each gate is essentially a hollow steel sector that can rotate — they call it a rising sector gate. When it’s down, it lies flat and out of the way. When it rotates up, it blocks the flow. There’s a nice balance there between functionality and not interfering with daily river use.

What makes it especially interesting is that it’s all about prediction and timing. You’re not reacting to water already in the city — you’re making a decision hours in advance, based on models, forecasts, and probabilities. Close it too often, and you disrupt shipping and river ecology. Close it too late, and the consequences are severe.

And here’s where it connects to what you were saying about prevention: the barrier has been closed far more often than originally expected. Partly due to better caution, partly due to rising sea levels. It’s doing its job, but it’s also a reminder that the assumptions you design around don’t stay fixed.

In a way, it’s the opposite of something like Tacoma Narrows. That was a failure that taught a lesson. The Thames Barrier is a success that quietly prevents one — over and over again, without most people ever noticing.

It’s the kind of project where, if you’ve done your job perfectly, nothing happens. Which, as you probably know, is sometimes the hardest thing to get people to appreciate.

The story of the St. Francis Dam in California, 1928.

It was designed by William Mulholland, a highly respected engineer—largely self-taught, but with a huge track record in building Los Angeles’ water system. The canyon walls were geologically complex—on one side, relatively solid rock; on the other, an ancient landslide area with much weaker, unstable material. There were also issues with water seepage through the abutments. Some leaks were observed, but they were interpreted as normal for a structure of that type.

On March 12, 1928, after the reservoir had been filled for only a short time, the dam failed catastrophically.

No warning that made it to the public. The structure gave way, and a wall of water rushed down the canyon, eventually reaching the Pacific Ocean nearly 50 miles away. Over 400 people were killed.

It wasn’t one glaring mistake; it was a chain of judgments that, individually, seemed acceptable, but together created a situation with very little margin for error.

It changed engineering practice in a way that might feel familiar to you: much more emphasis on geology, independent review, and not relying too heavily on a single person’s judgment, no matter how experienced.

Mulholland never really recovered. He took responsibility publicly and withdrew from professional life.
